questions.q: The agent picks the right skill 92% of the time in your offline test. Why is success still down?
questions.a: The choice happens on every turn. As an illustration with my own numbers: at 92% per turn, a 20-turn run with no wrong pick happens 0.92 multiplied by itself 20 times, about 19% of the time. It's guide 1's sum again.

questions.q: What if all 40 are really needed?
questions.a: Keep all 40 installed, but don't show them all. Anthropic suggests keeping your three to five most-used tools always loaded and letting search find the rest. Or show skills by project or by phase of the task.

teach.title: How it works: proving it, then fixing it

questions.q: Won't a smarter model fix it?
questions.a: It helps: Opus 4.5 started far above Opus 4. But the search step still added about 8.6 points on top. Better models shrink the problem; they haven't removed it.

teach.title: How it works: proving it, then fixing it

questions.q: Tokens are ruled out. What two costs of 40 skills remain?
questions.a: Choosing: wrong picks among look-alikes, on every turn. And hijacking: a wrongly opened skill's instructions steer the rest of the run.

questions.q: What does the equal-length filler control prove?
questions.a: If the same amount of text without extra skills doesn't hurt, while real skills do, then length isn't the cause. The number of choices is.

teach.title: How it works: proving it, then fixing it

questions.q: Name two fixes that keep every skill installed.
questions.a: A search step that shows only a few relevant skills per turn, and descriptions that say when not to use each skill (or showing skills only in the projects and phases where they apply).
